⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, most plants rely on real-time photosynthesis for food, which means they aren’t generating energy unless the sun is out.
  • Recent findings suggest that plants generally absorb carbon dioxide through pores in their leaves, but the prickly pear can’t afford such an evolutionary luxury.
  • Environmental biologists certainly did.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, most plants rely on real-time photosynthesis for food, which means they aren’t generating energy unless the sun is out. Meanwhile, cacti like the prickly pear must get creative in order to survive the harsh conditions they live in. With high temperatures and little water, these plants and similar species like aloe and pineapple evolved a specialized process called crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM). The overall principles are the same, but instead of converting carbon dioxide (CO₂) and water into sugars solely during daylight, CAM allows a prickly pear to extend its photosynthesis over a full 24 hours.

Recent findings suggest that plants generally absorb carbon dioxide through pores in their leaves, but the prickly pear can’t afford such an evolutionary luxury. The desert heat would turn those same tiny openings into water drains. With CAM, a prickly pear only absorbs carbon dioxide at night, and subsequently turns it into malic acid. Photosynthesis later breaks down the acid—but only on the side of the plant directly exposed to sunlight. The shady side retains its malic acid, creating a pH concentration gradient. Interestingly, this pH imbalance is also one of the underlying principles for generating electricity…see where this is going?

Environmental biologists certainly did. In a study published today in the journal Plants, People, Planet, a team at the University of California, Santa Cruz, (UC Santa Cruz) detailed a fresh, interdisciplinary system that transforms the common prickly pear into a green solar panel. Although prickly pear voltages aren’t enough to deliver a noticeable jolt, they are strong enough to power the tiny sensors often used by farmers to monitor their crops. With some additional fine-tuning, their novel methods could offer a promising, sustainable adaptation to ongoing climate concerns.

It has been revealed that “It was just so nice to have 10 students in a room from all across campus working together on a single project. When we’re looking at climate solutions, that’s what we need,” Charlie Chesney, a UC Santa Cruz environmental scientist and study co-author, remarked in a statement.

According to recent reports, wiring a single spiky plant doesn’t do much, but linking them together adds up. As few as eight prickly pears are enough to generate 4.5 volts of electricity—nearly three times the charge of a commercial AA battery. That’s more than enough to power the common, low-energy sensors used to assess plants.

“There are many commercial applications of cacti [for] monitoring their health using a low-power system like ours, that is just operating off on the side and is self-powered,” explained UC Santa Cruz ecologist and study co-author Michael Loik.

He offered one such scenario, where wired prickly pears function as organic “sentinels” that monitor field conditions and relay the information back to a farmer’s office.

“This could be a really interesting avenue to pursue,” he added.

The idea isn’t limited to the prickly pear, either. Any plant that uses CAM—aloe, pineapple, agave—could benefit from a similar battery upgrade. The team even assessed how the cacti performed under a standard desert challenge like drought. Even after 15 months without water, sample prickly pears weren’t simply surviving—they were still photosynthesizing. In some cases, the resultant voltages were higher than watered control plants.

“This was a really surprising result, but also showed how resilient a cactus is—it could still produce electricity even when it seems, to us, like it’s near death,” added Chesney.

Latest Update: The 'Fresh Start' Trap

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (980 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • We're just about a month away from the latest year, and many of us have started thinking about our goals for 2027.
  • In a recent development, the massive lure of a new year (or a birthday, or any milestone) is the promise that things will be completely different from now on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

We're just about a month away from the latest year, and many of us have started thinking about our goals for 2027. Even if you're not one for New Year's resolutions, you likely have a mental image of how you want the coming year to unfold.

In a recent development, the massive lure of a new year (or a birthday, or any milestone) is the promise that things will be completely different from now on. Researchers call this the fresh start effect: Temporal landmarks like these motivate us to pursue our aspirations. And I, for one, fall for it every single time. I've had a special relationship with planners and fancy diaries for as long as I can remember. When we travel, I have to visit stationery shops and buy at least one little thing for my excited inner child.

Recently, I went on the IKEA website to find a new desk. Instead, I spent an hour filling my cart with storage boxes and organizers I did not need. There's something about organization that feels like home at an almost spiritual level, as if my soul finally has a place to rest from the noise of life.

For many of us, and especially perfectionists, a fresh start offers that same sense of ease and flow. The problem is that the image we create in our minds has us transformed from a mere mortal into someone who has everything under control. There's no room for a bad day, for the unexpected, for confusion, uncertainty, or messy emotions.

This is why the fresh start strategy fails us year after year. I've known this for a long time, but only recently have I understood why it's doomed from the start, and what actually works instead.

First, the person starting fresh is the same person who has been struggling for decades. She hasn't built the emotional capacities she needs to keep going when things don't go her way. Mess and imperfection are bound to disrupt our internal state because we are wired for safety. Wiping the slate clean gives us the illusion of control and returns the body to a state of balance. But it leaves us just as vulnerable the next time around.

It has been revealed that second, starting over is an attempt to control life rather than to grow the capacity to meet it. The whole purpose of the exercise is to feel in charge of our lives, to no longer be so vulnerable to what comes our way. There's nothing wrong with that. Who wants to drift and whirl like a leaf every time the wind blows? But hanging on for dear life, judging every moment, and beating ourselves up for how we react doesn't get us far either.

Industry observers note that where I'm learning to live, more and more, is in that liberating place between drifting and starting over; where I don't have to go back to base when life happens, because I am no longer judging it. I can let things not go as planned, because where I am in that moment is where I am supposed to be. In the mess. And there's nothing wrong with it.

According to recent reports, of course, the perfectionist in me gets riled up. She tells me this kind of acceptance will make me complacent. That I will become the lazy, unmotivated creature we all secretly fear we are. That I will waste my life and one day wake up with regrets, when it's too late to do anything about it.

It has been revealed that if any of this feels true for you, I encourage you not to fight that voice. It's there for a reason, partly biological, partly experiential. Challenging it will not get you far. Worse, it will get in the way of accessing the other voice, the one in service of your best possible life. We all have it. Call it intuition, call it inner guidance, or call it what psychologist Richard Schwartz calls "Self" with a capital S.

But you cannot access it when fear has the mic turned up to full volume.

Industry observers note that so turn down the volume. Let the fear be. Slowly, you will hear the voice that tells you what you need to do, given where you are, to move in the right direction. She won't always speak in words. Sometimes it will be an image, or a feeling. Take it seriously if it feels right, even if it makes no promises.

Because that feeling has a power to it that "perfect" does not.

Industry observers note that start developing this voice as you go about your day. Bring her into the small decisions: what to eat, what to wear. Turn to her for the bigger decisions too, like whether to have a difficult conversation, or how to have it. The more you befriend her, the more you will live, this year, next year, and every year after, aligned with who you are and growing into who you can become.

As you think about 2027 and how you want your life to be, think also of who you need to become to live that life. Not the perfect, always-in-control version of you, but the one who can stay with the mess.

Sources indicate that what capacities will she need to develop? Perhaps sitting with uncertainty without rushing to fix it. Perhaps resting without guilt, or letting a bad day just be a bad day. Perhaps trusting her inner voice when it makes no promises.

Industry observers note that choose one. Then ask yourself: What is one small way I can start practicing it today, not on January 1st?

#121301. Industry News: BYD’s folding steering wheel isn’t a concept — it’s in a $49K SUV now

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1135 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: BYD’s folding steering wheel isn’t a concept — it’s in a $49K SUV now

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1135 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that BYD launched a production SUV today with a steering wheel that folds flat into the dashboard.
  • According to recent reports, automakers and suppliers have been parading folding wheels on concept cars for about a decade.
  • The whole thing hinges on steer-by-wire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that BYD launched a production SUV today with a steering wheel that folds flat into the dashboard. It comes standard on the top trim of the Fang Cheng Bao Tai 9, which sells for 329,900 yuan (about $49,000) in China.

According to recent reports, automakers and suppliers have been parading folding wheels on concept cars for about a decade. This is the first one customers can actually order, according to BYD.

The whole thing hinges on steer-by-wire. There’s no steering column physically connecting the wheel to the front wheels, so the wheel is just an input device, and BYD can put it wherever it wants.

On the Tai 9, it swings through 180 degrees on a hidden hinge and drops into a compartment in the dash in about 10 seconds. A panel closes over it, and a tray table folds out where the wheel used to be. Only the airbag remains outside of the compartment – keeping it useful with the steering wheel deployed or hidden.

It only folds when the vehicle is parked. Fang Cheng Bao pairs it with a driver’s seat that reclines to 165 degrees, so the pitch is simple: fold the wheel, lie back, and eat, nap, or play games while you charge or wait. The brand claims 80% of the driver’s area becomes usable space and rates the folding mechanism for 80,000 cycles.

When it’s deployed, it’s a regular D-shaped wheel with a full rim and physical buttons. No yoke. That’s a nice change from Tesla and Mercedes, which paired its new steer-by-wire system on the EQS with a yoke.

At the launch event, Fang Cheng Bao general manager Xiong Tianbo said the industry had been talking about folding steering wheels since 2016 without ever getting one into mass production. He added that BYD is using the same type of motor it develops for humanoid robots to move the wheel, a first in one of its cars.

Here’s Fang Cheng Bao’s official video of the feature:.

According to recent reports, china’s new national standard for steering systems took effect on July 1, 2026. It dropped the long-standing requirement for a mechanical link between the steering wheel and the road wheels, as long as the system meets redundancy and fail-safe rules.

In a recent development, before that, steer-by-wire needed special approval. Nio’s ET9 was the first car in China to get it, back in December 2024. In the US, Tesla’s Cybertruck already uses it, and Mercedes is bringing it to the EQS this year.

Recent findings suggest that folding wheels themselves have stayed on show stands. BYD’s own Denza brand demonstrated one on the Z concept at Shanghai in 2025. Autoliv and Tensor called theirs the “world’s first foldable steering wheel” at CES in January, for a Tensor Robocar they expected to reach volume production in the second half of 2026. Hyundai Mobis has been showing one for years.

Tesla went the other way with the Cybercab: no wheel at all. But the prototypes testing on public roads have a Cybertruck steering wheel bolted onto an exposed column, because a human still has to be able to drive.

The Tai 9 is Fang Cheng Bao’s biggest SUV yet. It’s 5,270 mm (207.5 in) long with a 3,130 mm wheelbase and six seats in a 2+2+2 layout. It’s also the first model on BYD’s newly introduced DMS hybrid platform.

According to recent reports, A 1.5-liter turbo engine works with front and rear electric motors for a combined 400 kW (536 hp), and 0 to 100 km/h takes 4.8 seconds. The 66.48 kWh second-generation Blade battery supports BYD’s flash charging and delivers 310 km (193 miles) of electric range on the WLTC cycle. Rear-wheel steering, LiDAR, and BYD’s God’s Eye B driver assistance system are standard.

There are three trims: 279,900 yuan (about $41,700), 299,900 yuan, and 329,900 yuan. Only the top one gets the folding wheel.

Fang Cheng Bao sold 43,872 vehicles in October, up 41% year-over-year, mostly on the strength of the Tai 7. That model is now heading overseas: BYD sells it in the UK as the Ti 7. BYD hasn’t remarked anything about exporting the Tai 9.

In a recent development, it is not only that these technologies are impressive, but it is the speed at which they are being put into market by some of these Chinese car companies like BYD. They are moving further and further away from the competition but its understandable with the insane competition between car makers in China that they almost have to maintain and edge.

In a recent development, we’ve seen this at pretty much every auto show since the mid-2010s: a steering wheel slides away so the “driver” can relax while the car drives itself. It never shipped, for many reasons, but with steer-by-wire and autonomous driving now becoming reality, BYD is making the jump.

The Tai 9’s wheel only folds when you’re parked, so right now it’s a lounge feature. Recline the seat, stow the wheel, flip out the tray, and watch a movie while you charge. Is that a gimmick? A little. But Chinese EV buyers spend a lot of time in parked cars, and fridges, screens, and lie-flat seats sell cars there for a reason.

Sources indicate that the bigger deal is underneath. The wheel can only fold because the Tai 9 is steer-by-wire, and BYD is putting that in a roughly $49,000 family SUV less than five months after China made it legal. After Cybertruck and now Mercedes with the EQS, we might be seeing the first steps of steer-by-wire actually becoming a more widely adopted technology.

#121300. How Insight Led to Gratitude

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (897 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

How Insight Led to Gratitude

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (897 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that as I celebrate Thanksgiving in 2026, I find countless things to be thankful for.
  • It has been revealed that the word “insight” can describe the recognition of a medical condition by the person who has the condition, particularly with a brain disorder like schizophrenia or bipolar disorder.
  • Today, living in recovery, I am not just thankful for the positive things in my life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Recent findings suggest that as I celebrate Thanksgiving in 2026, I find countless things to be thankful for. I have parents and friends, a great church, my college education, my work, and a spacious apartment near my alma mater, the University of Cincinnati. Everything I give thanks for in my life today was made possible by finding an effective antipsychotic medication that enabled me to develop insight into my schizophrenia in 2008. I have lived in full remission from schizophrenia ever since.

It has been revealed that the word “insight” can describe the recognition of a medical condition by the person who has the condition, particularly with a brain disorder like schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. The technical term for a lack of insight into a medical condition is “anosognosia.” Right hemispheric stroke patients often struggle with anosognosia. They may have a paralyzed limb, but when the doctor asks them to move their limb, they come up with excuses such as that they don’t feel like moving their limb at that time, entirely unaware they are paralyzed. Most people with schizophrenia suffer from anosognosia, at least at first. It is a hallmark of schizophrenia. This was my situation beginning in 2006, over a year before I was diagnosed with schizophrenia and began treatment.

Today, living in recovery, I am not just thankful for the positive things in my life. I am also deeply grateful for the most basic needs. A shower, a refrigerator, the safety of sleeping in a bed indoors, enough money to go out to eat when I like. For four years, while homeless due to untreated schizophrenia, these were things I didn’t have.

What isolation and estrangement do to a person.

According to recent reports, another thing I did not have when I was homeless due to untreated schizophrenia was family and friends involved in my life. Looking back, I was not aware that my isolation and estrangement from family were entirely due to my own paranoia. My parents had always supported me with kindness, love, and generosity. Today I am deeply grateful to have my parents in my life again and see them often.

According to recent reports, on March 3, 2007, my homelessness ended. That was the day when neighbors called the police on me for screaming back at the voices in my mind, and I was taken to a psychiatric hospital. I hated being in the hospital, but my medication made a huge difference. It eliminated my delusions, paranoia, and most of my hallucinations, and it also left me questioning why I had chosen to become homeless for four years.

Today, I live with healthy insight, aware that I have schizophrenia, which is in full remission on clozapine, and I know that my symptoms of schizophrenia would quickly return if I were to ever go off my antipsychotic, even for a few days. I also recognize that if I were to go off my clozapine, relapse, and then need to go back on it, it would likely not be nearly as effective as it is today. Unfortunately, many people don't see the danger of inconsistent medication compliance. During the last nearly two decades, I have not missed my clozapine doses. I am thankful that I have developed a level of insight that keeps me stable and healthy.

The connection between insight and thankfulness.

Looking back, I needed insight to perceive reality clearly enough to be thankful.

Recent findings suggest that I never take my apartment for granted, especially when it rains. I remember sleeping outside under a church overhang, getting soaked, with nowhere else to go.

Today, my refrigerator is filled with healthy food, including vegetables, lots of fresh fruit, and cooking supplies. I will never forget living without knowing where my next meal would come from, and worrying that the food I found would be contaminated and make me sick. I still remember accidently ingesting some metal chips on donuts I found near a construction site, which gave me continual abdominal pain for months.

It has been revealed that before I became homeless, I traveled to both Africa and Southeast Asia, but I didn’t bring enough money with me. I remember sleeping in the airport in Hong Kong during an 18-hour layover with no money for a hotel room. I also traveled to both places on my own and took risks, such as living in a slum area of Nairobi, which was highly dangerous for foreigners. During my illness, I felt no sense of danger, due to impaired insight. Today, I am grateful for a clear mind that helps me make smart decisions about my safety.

I am also grateful that I had the opportunity to return to the university and finish my degree, though my first doctors thought that would be highly unlikely.

Perhaps I am most grateful I learned from these horrible things and now give back to society. I have published two books which I use to encourage others and educate families about the experience of schizophrenia. Mind Estranged is a memoir on my illness and recovery, and Awakenings tells the stories of 28 people who, like me, are thriving despite schizophrenia.

  • “Cubs learn at their own pace, and thanks to amazing recreation sites like Anan, we get to witness their tiny triumphs up close,” the rangers write.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in bear life, as in human life, sometimes you just have to take a leap of faith. A brown bear (Ursus arctos) cub hanging around Anan Creek in Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska learned that this summer. Its mom, Gemini, was crossing the creek, and one cub jumped right in. But this cub? Not so sure. It stood waiting at the water’s edge, before jumping in.

For this forceful leap into the water, the park rangers have awarded Gemini’s little cub with the 2026 Yeet of Faith Award. For those keeping score at home, Gemini won this year’s helicopter mom award.

“Cubs learn at their own pace, and thanks to amazing recreation sites like Anan, we get to witness their tiny triumphs up close,” the rangers write.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Recent findings suggest that tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots for wildlife is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

Sources indicate that according to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears (Ursus americanus) and eight brown bears like Gemini and her cubs. Similar to their chubby counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to gorge on salmon ahead of the long winter, and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear around Anan Creek has their own habits and quirks.

Sources indicate that the U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behaviors.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, mid-year model automobiles are like safeties in football games: rare, but maybe not as uncommon as you might guess at first. But the latest in that tradition, the 2027.5 Volkswagen GTI Rabbit Edition, doesn’t just split the difference between 2027 and 2028; it also slides between the S and SE models that make up the lower tiers of the lineup, while bringing along some of the sweet features from the top-shelf GTI Autobahn trim. In other words, it has the makings of a Goldilocks special.

According to recent reports, first, a dash of history. “Rabbit” was the name originally used by VW for the Golf in the U.S. and Canadian markets back in the days of the Mk1, including on the first GTI that arrived in 1979 in the Great White North and in ‘83 in the States. (The firm then returned to the Rabbit name for the Mk5 Golf here, but that’s less consequential—or memorable.) In honor of that first GTI, this new trim includes an adorable little chrome bunny on its hatch, in addition to blacked-out mirror caps, grille, and other trim bits scattered around the exterior that replace red items on other members of the current GTI family.

The GTI Rabbit Edition also boasts the first North American use of Dark Moss Green Metallic, a paint job previously reserved for Europe’s Golf GTI Edition 50 that set the front-wheel drive Nurburgring lap record. The 19-inch black wheels come from the Golf R, and are wrapped as standard in summer performance tires, versus the all-season rubber that normally comes with less-expensive GTIs. But the most notable change on the fun side is the presence of the DCC adaptive dampers, for which you otherwise would have to spring for the top-shelf Autobahn trim to get. Inside, meanwhile, the Rabbit Edition picks up the GTI SE’s GTI Clubsport ArtVelours material on its comfy yet supportive front buckets and rear bench.

Like all other current GTIs, unfortunately, the Rabbit Edition forces buyers to use a seven-speed dual-clutch automatic to change the gears tied to its 241-horsepower turbocharged inline-four; the manual gearbox remains locked in the past. Still, if you can look past that, the Rabbit Edition has the makings of a steal. Volkswagen hasn’t revealed pricing yet—that’ll come closer to its on-sale date of Q2 2027—but seeing as how the carmaker is quite explicit about where it lands in the lineup, expect it to come in the $36,250 of the GTI S and the $40,240 of the GTI SE, plus or minus any little price bumps they might pick up in the next half model year.

Hyundai’s IONIQ 5 is the most popular EV in the US this year through September that isn’t a Tesla, ranking third behind the Model Y and Model 3.

Latest Update: Nearly 3 million pages of military records from the War of 1812 are finally online

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (504 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that after 16 years of painstaking work, the National Archives and its collaborators have finally completed digitizing over 90,000 pension applications submitted to the United States government following the War of 1812.
  • While archivists previously digitized a similar collection related to the American Revolutionary War, the upcoming documents will help fill in knowledge gaps between early 19th century military events and the 1850 federal census.
  • “In the specific case of the War of 1812 pension records, there is an added priority due to their frail state where not acting may mean sacrificing these for future generations,” Oxley noted in a recent announcement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that after 16 years of painstaking work, the National Archives and its collaborators have finally completed digitizing over 90,000 pension applications submitted to the United States government following the War of 1812. The project is more than just preservation for preservation’s sake. The roughly 2.8 million pages contain long-forgotten and missing details about 19th century Americans, their families, and their everyday lives.

While archivists previously digitized a similar collection related to the American Revolutionary War, the upcoming documents will help fill in knowledge gaps between early 19th century military events and the 1850 federal census. Patricia Oxley, president of the Federation of Genealogical Societies (FGS), explained the project was also incredibly time-sensitive.

“In the specific case of the War of 1812 pension records, there is an added priority due to their frail state where not acting may mean sacrificing these for future generations,” Oxley noted in a recent announcement.

The somewhat upcoming United States of America declared war on the United Kingdom on June 18, 1812, citing objections to trade restrictions with France amid the Napoleonic Wars, as well as the Royal Navy’s impressment of American sailors. Although the conflict famously included a British attack on Washington D.C. that resulted in the burning of the White House and U.S. Capitol, little shifted geopolitically between the two nations following the ratification of the Treaty of Ghent on February 17, 1815. The U.S. tallied around 15,000 casualties, while the U.K. and Canada saw about 10,700 deaths. Another 9,000 Indigenous fighters died while enlisted between the two sides.

Today’s military records are meticulously documented and stored digitally, but applying for benefits such as pensions was a much more labor-intensive process during the 19th century. With the burden of proof on each applicant, veterans were required to supply lengthy accounts of their service. Each War of 1812 pension file is liable to contain not just combat information, but the names and personal details of fellow soldiers, family members, spouses, and countless other relations.

“Our people have been asking for the War of 1812 pension records for some time, and I expect this collection to be very popular based on the rich war time detail it contains,” added Brian Hansen, general manager at Fold3, Ancestry’s military records service and National Archives collaborator.

Industry observers note that the collection also includes a full-text search feature using handwriting recognition technology. This lets owners explore the files based on every named individual, and not simply the primary veteran applicants. The pension records are at the moment available for free on Fold3’s website, and are being added to the National Archives catalog on a rolling basis.

Correction 11/20/26 9:30 a.m. EST: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated the pension archive contained around 7 million files. This was based on an initial assessment from researchers in 2010. The article has been updated to reflect the more accurate tally.

#121294. How to Stand Out As Authentic in a World of AI

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (677 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

How to Stand Out As Authentic in a World of AI

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (677 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.
  • In today’s world, much of what we used to do manually is automated—which, in many cases, saves time that we can spend with friends and loved ones.
  • In a recent development, but there is good news.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

In today’s world, much of what we used to do manually is automated—which, in many cases, saves time that we can spend with friends and loved ones. Yet artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved beyond automation. In many industries, it has become personalized and interactive, able to establish relationships. Artificial rapport can lead to unhealthy attachment, which becomes dangerous when it replaces human relationships. As I explain in a TEDx talk on “The Honeymoon Phase of Artificial Intelligence,”[i] in some cases, AI has gone rogue as a digital intimate and led emotionally vulnerable young people to make tragic decisions, relying on harmful “advice” from their computerized confidants.

In a recent development, but there is good news. Research corroborates what most people understand instinctively: we innately prefer human contact to artificial. This makes sense, considering we are warned to avoid anything artificial: from artificial friendships in the workplace to artificially inflated prices in the marketplace. Within relationships, we prefer authenticity even when recognizing AI might deliver better “answers.” Research explains.

It has been revealed that joshua D. Wenger et al. (2026) examined the human preference for human empathy, despite ranking AI empathy as higher in quality.[ii] In four studies, they investigated whether people prefer expressions of empathy from real people or AI. They discovered evidence for what they referred to as the “AI empathy choice paradox”—the finding that participants preferred human empathy yet perceived AI-generated empathy as higher quality and more effective at helping them feel heard. In other words, although people may avoid seeking empathy from AI, they benefit from it when they experience it. Wenger et al. therefore suggest that AI could supplement human emotional support, rather than replace it.

Recent findings suggest that tobias Kleinert et al. (2026) investigated whether people engaging in an emotional discussion preferred a conversation partner who was a real person or artificial intelligence (AI).[iii] They studied 492 participants who engaged online through a method designed to facilitate rapid relationship building, with conversation partners who were either human or AI. They found that AI-generated content outperformed human-generated content in establishing closeness during emotionally engaging interactions, including topics such as the most valued aspect of a friendship or a most treasured life memory. Being explicitly informed they would be interacting with AI, however, created an anti-AI bias, which reduced relationship building, though not to the point of elimination. Kleinert et al. attribute this reduction to participants having less motivation to engage with AI, a fact which was bolstered by reduced feelings of closeness and shorter responses.

Sources indicate that we can enhance interpersonal relationships by harnessing the best of both worlds: adopting AI qualities such as active listening and emotionally appropriate encouragement, coupled with authentic presence through proximity, eye contact, and a soft expression. Indeed, Kleinert et al. note that humans generally prefer human partners when seeking emotional interactions. They note that human-AI interactions usually satisfy concrete social needs such as pleasure, instead of deeper, symbolic needs such as experiencing the feeling of genuine care. They note that people share a basic, evolutionary drive for social connection that includes mutual understanding, shared emotions, and the comfort of companionship with someone who truly understands our feelings.

Industry observers note that we can enhance our ability to be a good listener and emotionally supportive partner when we recognize the rationale behind the preference for personal human contact. And the proliferation of automation and artificial assistance continues to create a preference for reality.

[i] https://youtu.be/14KiWy5XvYk?si=VMoIkLwJFPIoOHEz.

[ii] Wenger, Joshua D., C. Daryl Cameron, and Michael Inzlicht. “People Choose to Receive Human Empathy despite Rating AI Empathy Higher.” Communications Psychology (London) 4, no. 1 (2026): 19.

[iii] Kleinert, Tobias, Marie Waldschütz, Julian Blau, Markus Heinrichs, and Bastian Schiller. “AI Outperforms Humans in Establishing Interpersonal Closeness in Emotionally Engaging Interactions, but Only When Labelled as Human.” Communications Psychology (London) 4, no. 1 (2026): 23.

#121291. Melissa Joan Hart Explains It All: Hot Flashes, Menopause, and Turning 50

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (942 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

Melissa Joan Hart Explains It All: Hot Flashes, Menopause, and Turning 50

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that actor Melissa Joan Hart has a vivid memory of her mother standing in front of their open freezer to cool off.
  • Sources indicate that “[She’s] only 20 years older than me, so maybe I missed the part where she was going through [menopause], but there was no conversation about it,” Hart told Healthline.
  • Her own perimenopausal symptoms started with night sweats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that actor Melissa Joan Hart has a vivid memory of her mother standing in front of their open freezer to cool off. As a child, she didn’t understand why. Now, as a 50-year-old woman, Hart knows that her mom was experiencing hot flashes.

Sources indicate that “[She’s] only 20 years older than me, so maybe I missed the part where she was going through [menopause], but there was no conversation about it,” Hart told Healthline. “I feel like it’s just becoming a hot topic with women, where…the taboo is going away from it now.”.

Her own perimenopausal symptoms started with night sweats.

“[It] was really jarring, and the first few times, you’re not really sure what that was…do I need to turn the air down or what’s going on here?” Hart mentioned.

Over time, she learned that she was experiencing moderate to severe hot flashes, which affect up to 80% of women during the menopause transition and can persist for 7 to 10 years.

Doctors categorize hot flashes as mild, moderate, or severe, mentioned Diana Bitner, MD, OB-GYN, at Corewell Health.

According to recent reports, “[So] if they’re mild, it’s a sense of warmth (maybe in the chest, or the neck, or the face). A moderate hot flash is where there’s associated sweating, and a severe hot flash is something that stops you in your tracks, wakes you up from the middle of the night,” Bitner told Healthline.

Hart has mostly experienced hot flashes while home or at her three sons’ activities, and they have yet to interfere with her work. However, according to research, one in three women report moderate to severe challenges in managing their work due to symptoms related to menopause.

“It’s just so sad that about 10% of women leave the workforce due to menopause,” said Bitner. “And so it can really affect our ability to perform at these key years of not only institutional memory, but also of earning power, and it can really affect the whole community.”.

Bitner noted women should feel empowered to bring up their menopausal symptoms or questions with their doctor.

In a recent development, “[This] is something that was taboo for so long…women didn’t really talk about this, whether it was because of embarrassment, or [they] weren’t sure if anyone was experiencing it,” she stated. “[There’s] no reason, in this day and age, we need to suffer through it…it’s something that there are treatment options for.”.

In fact, Bitner mentioned providing specific details about their symptoms, such as how many mild, moderate, or severe hot flashes they’ve experienced over the past week, can help doctors better assess patients’ needs.

Hart prepares to discuss treatment options for her hot flashes with her doctor soon. In the last few years, she noted she has put emphasis on her midlife health.

“I just was sick of waking up with aches and pains in general [thinking], ‘is this the rest of my life?’” she noted.

She started listening to self-help books in the car while driving her kids around and found ways to put herself first.

“My kids are a little bit older, so I kind of have that freedom to be able to do that,” she said. “[But] along with getting older, comes the menopause, comes that different time in life. And I think it’s a good time to reevaluate [how] our bodies can’t handle what [they] used to handle, and let’s figure it out.”.

Hart has partnered with pharmaceutical company Bayer on its “Life Doesn’t Stop for a Hot Flash” campaign, which encourages women to discuss menopause symptoms with their doctors and promotes Lynkuet, a hormone-free prescription medication for moderate to severe hot flashes associated with menopause.

“It’s called ‘Life Doesn’t Stop for a Hot Flash’ campaign because it shouldn’t, because we should be able to push through, and this should be a time in our lives when our kids are getting older, and we’re able to kind of reinvent ourselves,” said Hart. “And I think it’s an exciting time, and it shouldn’t be something that we’re afraid of.”.

She is embracing speaking openly about midlife health.

“I hit 50 this year, and it was, like, a huge milestone, and I think that’s something to be proud of, and not something to shy away from,” she mentioned.

Hart also hopes to challenge the longstanding barriers women face in Hollywood as they age, including fewer opportunities for leading roles.

“[I] think we’re seeing that the generation before, and my generation, it feels like we’re pushing those boundaries…and we’re saying, you know, that women at this age have a lot to give, have a lot of information to share, have a lot of stories to tell and experiences and adventures still ahead of us, and, you know, we’re not ready to stop,” Hart said.

In everyday life, Bitner mentioned that while some patients avoid talking about midlife challenges like menopause with their doctors, she is seeing more patients who are confident being forthcoming.

According to recent reports, as more women talk openly about menopause, she hopes to include men in the conversation, too. In fact, she invites her patients to bring their partners to appointments, so they can gain an understanding of menopause and the experiences their partners face, such as hot flashes, sleep issues, vaginal dryness, and discomfort or pain during intercourse.

Sources indicate that “[Often], there’s, you know, comments that come up [from men who] say, ‘How do I talk about this without getting in trouble?’” stated Bitner. “[We] want everyone to join this conversation…it doesn’t have to be just her glitch because we know it’s not.”.

Antonelli Takes Pole Position in Las Vegas, Verstappen Inherits P1 with Grid Penalty

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Max Verstappen, who held provisional pole until the final flurry of attempts, will inherit the P1 starting spot, and George Russell will start second after qualifying third.
  • Russell, by far the fastest in Friday’s practice, asked the Mercedes pit wall if he could have a tow, knowing Mercedes was the clear frontrunner and his champion teammate was destined to start further back in the field.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that kimi Antonelli took pole for the Las Vegas Grand Prix by being the last of the contenders to start their final flying lap in Q3. With a five-place grid drop, the newly introduced F1 champion will start Saturday night’s Grand Prix from sixth.

Max Verstappen, who held provisional pole until the final flurry of attempts, will inherit the P1 starting spot, and George Russell will start second after qualifying third.

Russell, by far the fastest in Friday’s practice, asked the Mercedes pit wall if he could have a tow, knowing Mercedes was the clear frontrunner and his champion teammate was destined to start further back in the field.

Mercedes didn’t oblige, and both drivers entered the waiting game with the rest of the contenders, as no one wanted to be the first driver out for the final lap, punching through the frigid cold air of the Las Vegas desert alone.

According to recent reports, ultimately, Verstappen went first and did not improve on his first Q3 time, which was still good enough for an elevated front-row starting spot. Antonelli crossed the line to start his lap with a second remaining.

It has been revealed that lando Norris will start third after qualifying fourth ahead of Isack Hadjar and Arvid Lindblad. Oscar Piastri found himself in a familiar starting position of seventh but faces a 10-place grid penalty.

With rain on Thursday and a dry forecast for every session of consequence during the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend, most contenders first saw what their fresh 2027 cars had during FP3 on Friday, ahead of qualifying.

Neither Ferrari made it to Q3, settling for 11th and 12th as neither Lewis Hamilton nor Charles Leclerc put themselves in position to give the other a tow.

Nico Hulkenberg, Carlos Sainz, Gabriel Bortoleto, and Alex Albon were knocked out in Q2.

Turn off reality TV and turn on the bald eagle cams. It’s all the drama you need.

When internet-famous bald eagle Shadow seemingly welcomed a mysterious latest female into his nest earlier this week, many fans have questioned the whereabouts of Kaydee. After the death of Shadow’s longtime partner Jackie in August, he had been spotted spending time with the 4-year-old banded female eagle named KD1 (later renamed Kaydee). It seemed like the eagles might head into mating season as a pair, but after the arrival of a new, large female, it’s unclear how the relationships will all shake out.

Since the appearance of the mystery female, nicknamed Big Beautiful Visitor or BBV by some fans, Kaydee has disappeared from view of Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV)’s two cameras. She was last spotted by the cameras on November 14 in the Roost Tree, according to FOBBV. Despite concerns that she may be injured or had left the area, wildlife photographers have continued to document Kaydee’s presence near Big Bear Lake as recently as November 18.

Photographer Alla Shumko shared photos of Kaydee perched near Major Bear Lake on November 18. Kaydee’s double bands are visible as she observed a scuffle between younger eagles fighting over fish.

According to recent reports, mating season is well underway, so viewers of FOBBV’s 24/7 livecams have been watching closely for signs that Shadow has selected a upcoming partner. Shadow has worked with both Kaydee and the new eagle on nest maintenance and shared “beaky kisses” with each female, both signs of bonding in bald eagles. Bald eagle mating involves a bit of aerial acrobatics—copulating pairs can be seen in what’s called a “cartwheel display,” in which they lock talons in mid-air while tumbling down to the ground. Male eagles do not have an external phallus, so mating occurs via a touch of cloacas. Vocalizations can typically be heard during the act, which lasts about 7 to 12 seconds, according to Raptor Resource.

As this is nature, we humans can’t predict or influence who Shadow will pick as a upcoming partner. Or if he picks at all. All we can do is watch and wait and let nature take its course.

#121287. Breaking: What Babies Can Teach Us About Well-Being

Breaking: What Babies Can Teach Us About Well-Being

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1004 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.
  • According to recent reports, my wife and I had a baby earlier this year, and it has revolutionized my well-being.
  • In a recent development, when babies are born, they can only see about 20-30 cm away, and their vision is restricted to black and white.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

According to recent reports, my wife and I had a baby earlier this year, and it has revolutionized my well-being. She is a blessing, and I want to share with you five lessons she’s taught me.

In a recent development, when babies are born, they can only see about 20-30 cm away, and their vision is restricted to black and white. Basically, they can recognize a high-contrast boob, and that’s about it. They need to trust the people around them to take care of them, and they let you do it. Newborns don’t need training or trust funds; they just need to be confident that they’re loved and cared for.

It has been revealed that life flourishes when we offer love generously. We don’t expect customer service, or even reciprocity. We just want to see something thrive. This sentiment, when extended more widely, creates what I call a karmic culture. We help people because we want to live in the sort of world where people are cared for. When we need care, somebody else will be there to offer it to us. This creates a sense of safety, which promotes our thriving as much as it does a baby’s.

In a recent development, my daughter likes to start the day by letting one rip. After a long nap compressed in the sling, she will similarly greet consciousness by passing gas. Ah, sweet relief. My wife and I joke that she’s a very sincere person.

There’s a lesson here. Babies don’t care what other people think of them. They certainly don’t care what’s cool or rude; they’re just following their intrinsic motivations. Now I’m not suggesting that you should be an inconsiderate bore—offending people will undermine your relationships and thus, your well-being. But it is helpful to be in touch with what you authentically want to do with your life.

In the early, midsummer days of sleep deprivation, I would relieve my wife of the night shift around 6 a.m. and take baby out in the stroller. Mum needed sleep but would be set off by every noise in the house, so to the park we went, and it became a habit.

Sources indicate that as my daughter’s vision developed, I noticed her staring dumbfounded at the trees overhead. She was lost in the moment. She recently spent a good five minutes watching the autumn-coloured leaves on a bush rustle in the wind.

According to recent reports, I’d done something similar in the spring, watching a tree shimmer in the golden hour. But I had to make a conscious effort to stop, be wonderstruck, and stay mindful of the experience. I was reacting to scientific literature on the power of awe for well-being and trying to find the experience in the often-underwhelming urban environment in which I live. My daughter just did it automatically. Baby is wired for well-being. Be like baby.

It has been revealed that babies know the importance of rest and recovery. After a good meal and some color flash cards for brain development or a gym session ripping apart tissues, baby isn’t blue-lighting herself or otherwise hitting the dopamine button. She’s finding a dark corner in momma’s bosom and taking a nap.

Our sleep hygiene is under threat from screens, bad diets, excessive substance use, and life stresses. People are turning to sleep tracking apps, but the irony is that you’re just contaminating your sleep space with your phone. We’re taught to give babies a dark, quiet room with a cool temperature and zero stimulus. You can do the same for yourself. Sweet dreams.

In a recent development, when a friend’s older baby visited us last year, I studied with curiosity how much she enjoyed playing with the things in her mum’s handbag. She spent a good 15 minutes with a packet of wet wipes. Turning it over in her hands, tasting it, following Arnold Schwarzenegger’s advice to lift “down…up…” with “more energy!” She particularly enjoyed crinkling the packaging and listening to the crunchy sound it made.

Sources indicate that babies have a high degree of mindfulness and focus. Their baseline level of stimulus isn’t the slot machine Instagram feed or a 300-frames-per-second, cutting-edge video game. They can find joy in the everyday.

In a recent development, you can too. Indeed, it’s a great way to practice savoring, a well-established technique for increasing the frequency and extending the duration of good moods. Notice things that you enjoy regularly but don’t pay attention to, like your morning coffee, favorite sweater, or how pretty your houseplants are. Take a little longer to appreciate them. Really luxuriate in the sensations and emotions they evoke in you.

Meaning and purpose in life can be enhanced by the sense that you are contributing to something bigger than yourself, and few things bring that sense home quite as powerfully as raising another human.

A key theme of terror management theory is that humans are afraid of death. We create elaborate cultural practices either to convince ourselves of immortality, as the Pharaohs did, or to feel connected to something that will persist after our death, like a nation for which we die in battle. In my experience, your baby connects you to eternity; there is a strong sense that this being carries a part of you into the future.

I am reminded of the poetry of Kalil Gibran, On Children:.

Sources indicate that and a woman who held a babe against her bosom said, Speak to us of Children. And he said: Your children are not your children. They are the sons and daughters of Life’s longing for itself.

You may give them your love but not your thoughts, For they have their own thoughts. You may house their bodies but not their souls, For their souls dwell in the house of tomorrow.

#121286. Lifting Heavy Isn’t the Whole Story When It Comes to Building Strength. Here's What to Do Instead.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2390 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Lifting Heavy Isn’t the Whole Story When It Comes to Building Strength. Here's What to Do Instead.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2390 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My name is Cori Ritchey, and I am an exercise physiology nerd turned fitness journalist, and the fitness editor at Women’s Health.
  • It has been revealed that scroll any fitness feed and you’ll see it: people clanging plates, chasing PRs, and even pulling dangerous stunts for the pride of lifting heavy.
  • As a strength and conditioning coach and the fitness editor at Women’s Health, I’ve been preaching the lift-heavy-or-go-home gospel for years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My name is Cori Ritchey, and I am an exercise physiology nerd turned fitness journalist, and the fitness editor at Women’s Health. When I’m not writing, editing, and researching fitness, I’m teaching it to my personal training and group fitness clients. In my latest column, Between Sets, I’m pulling back the curtain on the same advice, tips, and ‘aha!’ moments I share with my clients while they’re catching their breath. Stick around for the strategic, science-backed nuggets that’ll help you move better, train smarter, and actually enjoy the process.

It has been revealed that scroll any fitness feed and you’ll see it: people clanging plates, chasing PRs, and even pulling dangerous stunts for the pride of lifting heavy. And where there’s real joy in getting stronger, there’s also real pressure to keep adding weight.

As a strength and conditioning coach and the fitness editor at Women’s Health, I’ve been preaching the lift-heavy-or-go-home gospel for years. For valid reason: challenging your muscles over time is one of the most reliable ways to build lasting strength, support bone health, improve body composition, and stay functional as we age.

The “lift heavy” ethos isn’t newly introduced. Strength training is as old as Ancient Greece, where the first gyms were developed. It progressed through decades of physical culture into Muscle Beach, USA, the birthplace of American lifting that started as a beachside gymnastics park in Venice Beach, California, in the 1940s. It was there, too, where the first American women bodybuilders, like legendary Abbey Stockton, emerged—at a time when many scientists still believed lifting was bad for the body.

Sources indicate that research eventually caught up to what lifters were already experiencing: resistance training works. More women, especially in recent years, started showing up for it, too. In 2004, 17 percent of women reported regularly participating in weight lifting. By 2020, that number has bumped to nearly 30 percent. Then came the influencer era, amplifying a message that’s equal parts motivating and misleading: lifting weights is good for you—but it has to be heavy to count.

In a recent development, there’s a kernel of truth in there. Progressive overload (the process of gradually increasing the stress you put on your body in a workout) builds muscle and strength, and increasing load is an efficient way to do so.

And that matters—especially when heavier, heavier, heavier simply isn’t in the cards.

In a recent development, because for many, it’s not. It requires access to specific equipment, time to train consistently without rushing through sets, and quality coaching and information to nail form and stay injury-free. It also has to be safe and appropriate for your body on any given day—whether you’re navigating chronic illness, postpartum or perimenopause realities, and injury history, or limiting pain. And even when everything lines up on paper, there’s a very real mental hurdle: walking into a gym and loading up a bar can be intimidating as hell.

Still, if you’re here to build strength, change your body composition, protect your bone health, or invest in your movement longevity, lifting heavier will certainly help—but it’s not the only path to lifelong strength. Somewhere along the way, “heavy” became synonymous with “effective”, and “light” or "moderate" became codes for “waste of time.”.

The exercise research world is finding that’s not the case. “You don't need to do anything heavy for the health benefits of resistance exercise to take place,” states Stuart Phillips, PhD, kinesiology professor and hypertrophy researcher at McMaster University.

Adequate research has suggested that hypertrophy (the fancy scientific term for muscle growth) is not determined by a magic rep goal or the weight on the bar, states Susie Reiner, PhD, CSCS, is an exercise physiologist, assistant professor of exercise science at Seton Hall University, and CEO of TheoryEx, a sport science research and consulting firm. “Instead, hypertrophy appears to be driven by whether a training set provides a sufficiently strong internal stimulus to the muscle, which is reasonably defined as effort and proximity to muscular failure.”.

Recent findings suggest that trainers have traditionally been taught that specific rep ranges map neatly to specific goals: 1 to 3 for power, 3 to 8 for strength, 8 to 12 for muscle, and 12-plus for muscular endurance. But newer findings show you can build muscle across a much wider rep range—roughly as low as 5 and as high as 25, Phillips indicates. “There is, then, by definition, no sweet spot for muscle building, because the whole repetition range then becomes the sweet spot.”.

Across several studies and meta-analyses, similar muscle growth has been seen between people who train with lighter loads (about 30 to 40 percent of their one-rep maximum), and those who train with heavier loads (about 70 to 85 percent of their one-rep maximum)—as long as sets are taken close enough to failure.

Muscle growth is dependent on recruiting and fatiguing a large portion of muscle fibers, Reiner notes. Your muscles need a reason to adapt. With heavier weights for fewer reps, you recruit a lot of fibers immediately. With lighter weights for higher reps, you recruit them more gradually.

According to recent reports, one thing to note here: while a large percentage of these studies have only been done in men, Phillips notes that “the work that has been done in women highlights us that actually men and women respond very, very similarly to weight lifting in terms of muscle mass gain. Women have less baseline muscle, but relatively speaking, they gain the same amount as men—that's been robustly shown.” Phillips and his colleagues are currently running several studies (including one study specific to perimenopausal women!) that will further clarify what this looks like in women.

Researchers feel confident that as long as sets are taken sufficiently to failure (more on what that means coming up), different loading strategies can produce similar hypertrophy, Reiner says.

Industry observers note that here’s what that looks like IRL: Let’s say you have biceps curls on your workout plan each week. One week, you pick up the 10-pound dumbbells, and do 3 sets of 12 reps. In the sets, when you approach the end of that rep range, it feels tough—you can maybe grind out 2 more reps max. The next week, you reach for the 15s. You can only hit 6 reps before you feel like your form is faltering, but the effort feels similar—you’ve still got about two reps left before your form breaks down.

The heavier weight might feel more empowering, but both workouts deliver a similar muscle-building stimulus—assuming you’re training regularly enough, eating enough protein and calories, and adequately recovering, of course.

Industry observers note that sure, research confirms you don’t have to lift crazy heavy—but that doesn’t mean that coming close to failure feels easy. Failing a rep can be scary (and honestly, discouraging). Here’s the good news: you don’t need true, all-out failure. You just need to train to proximity to failure.

It has been revealed that one practical way to gauge that is with the rate of perceived exertion scale. “Rate of perceived exertion (RPE) is a global effort scale, typically ranging from one to 10,” Reiner claims. An RPE of 10 represents maximal effort—no chance you could do one more rep. A RPE of nine suggests you could do one more, an RPE of eight means you could probably do two more reps, and so on and so forth.

Muscle growth still occurs between RPE of 7 to 9, Phillips says. “You don’t need it to be a 10 out of 10 where you’re red-lining and can’t get the bar off your chest.” In other words: you can train hard without routinely hitting the point where things get sketchy.

That matters, because the closer you get to all-out failure, the more your injury risk can creep up—especially if you start twisting, bouncing, and compensating to force a rep you simply don’t have.

It has been revealed that the failure you want to flirt with is technical failure, or technical fatigue. “Technical failure means you cannot complete another repetition with good form,” Phillips says—that’s where injury risk rises. Muscular failure (otherwise known as momentary failure) occurs when a muscle is unable to generate enough force to complete another rep, regardless of maximal effort. Picture trying to do one more biceps curl and you quite literally cannot lift your arm and the weight up again—that’s muscular failure..

According to recent reports, aim for technical failure. Pushing yourself too far in an effort to achieve muscular failure could cause your body to overcompensate and push you into a compromising position. The good news, too, is technical failure tends to be very close to muscular failure for most people, Phillips says.

A useful rule of thumb: stop when you have one to two perfect-form reps left in the tank.

Sources indicate that yes, you still need to reach for that RPE of 7 to 9—but there’s more ways to do that than just reaching for the next highest weight. Here are some other elements you can play with to up the challenge:.

Frequency. Reaching for heavier weights, you can simply aim to reach for any type of weight more often. That might look like increasing your strength training days from two to three days a week.

According to recent reports, volume. Think of your training volume as the amount of weight total you lift during a given session. Sure, lifting heavier loads is one way to increase your total, but it can also be accomplished by increasing the amount of sets or reps you do.

Rest time. Decreasing the amount of rest you allow yourself gives your muscles less time to recover, wearing them out quicker with lighter loads.

Time under tension. The amount of time your muscles work for matters. Increasing your time under tension, or the amount of time your muscles are working in a lift (for example, lowering a curl for a slow four-count).

It has been revealed that that all being said, heavier loads might still take the cake in terms of efficiency. You’ll find yourself increasing your frequency and volume to monotonous levels if you never increase your load.

Recent findings suggest that back to biceps curls: Say you get comfortable at six reps at 15 lbs. After a few weeks, it no longer starts to feel challenging for you, so you increase it eight. And then 10. And then 12. If you never reach for the intimidating 20 lb dumbbells, you’ll eventually find yourself having to do sets of 30 reps just to feel something. And that can become time consuming. You don’t need extremes all the time—but you do need your training to stay challenging.

“For individuals who are uncomfortable training to very high levels of effort, consistent training at moderate-to-high RPEs combined with sufficient volume and progression can still produce meaningful muscle growth,” Reiner says. “From a long-term perspective, hypertrophy depends less on any single maximal set and more on repeated exposure to challenging, well-managed training over weeks and months.”.

Convinced to start pushing closer to failure? Here are a few ways to progress safely.

Sources indicate that the two-for-two method is a classic progression strategy used by professional trainers. Once you can do two extra proper-form reps beyond your planned rep target for two workouts in a row, you’re ready to increase your load.

Sources indicate that let's use the biceps curl example just one more time. You’ve been training with the 15s for sets of 8, and now you can hit 10 with clean form for two workouts in a row. That’s your cue to grab 17.5s the next go.

How much should you increase, exactly? The National Strength and Conditioning Association’s guideline is 2.5 to 5 pounds for upper-body exercises, and 5 to 10 pounds for lower-body exercises. Reminder that this is just a general guide—you can do more or less based on how you specifically feel.

Trying heavier weights is way less intimidating when you have a safety net.

According to recent reports, if you’re nervous, ask for a spot. Maybe you already have a gym buddy you workout with regularly that can help pull the barbell up if you get stuck on a bench press. If you don’t, ask one of your gym’s trainers or employees. Most people will politely oblige, and will even appreciate your effort in challenging yourself.

Have a conversation with your spotter before you get into the lift. Tell them how many reps you’re aiming for, and a cue you’ll give them when you want them to jump in and help (my go-to is a simple “now”—since that’s about all you can get out when you’re out of breath).

Some days just don’t feel as strong as others. Maybe you didn’t sleep super well last night, stressed about work, or are at a tough point in your cycle. That’s life. When that happens, you need to respect the cues your body gives you.

If your warmup sets feel unusually heavy, take the hint: this just might not be the day to pick up that heavy weight. It doesn’t mean you’ve regressing, it’s just a bump in the road. Strength, and muscle building, is not a linear process.

Build muscle with the WH+ Build & Burn series.

Ultimately, building and maintaining muscle mass is one of the strongest investments you can make in long-term health—especially as you age.

Recent findings suggest that and lifting heavy is one effective way to provide muscle-building stimulus to the body—but it isn’t accessible, comfortable, or safe for everyone all the time. The goal is progressive challenge, and lighter loads can deliver that when you train with intention and effort.

It has been revealed that “You do not need to lift heavy to build muscle, but you do need to train with intention,” Reiner says. “The best approach is the one that someone can perform consistently, safely, and with enough effort to challenge the muscle over time.”.

She’s reported on topics regarding health, nutrition, mental health, fitness, sex, and relationships for several years. You can find more of her work in Men’s Health, HealthCentral, Livestrong, Self, and others.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, kia’s EV lineup covers just about every size and price point, but it believes one thing is still missing: a truly cheap electric car. That’s about to change in 2027, when Kia plans to unveil a fresh EV that could start at around $22,000 to $24,000.

It’s been 40 years since Kia introduced its first electric vehicle, the Besta EV, created so runners in the 1986 Asian Games wouldn’t have to breathe toxic fumes from the broadcast vehicle.

Kia has come a long way since the Besta EV hit the road, now offering a complete lineup of electric vehicles, from compact SUVs and hatchbacks to vans and three-row SUVs.

In Europe and the UK, Kia’s electric lineup consists of the EV2, EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, EV9, and PV5 van, but the Korean automaker isn’t done yet.

“With no intention of resting on its laurels,” Kia said, the brand intends to complete development of its first software-defined vehicle (SDV) by the end of 2027, an all-new B-segment EV hatchback.

It didn’t offer any other details on the upcoming EV, but Ted Lee, Kia’s executive vice president and head of global operations, told Auto Express that Kia and Hyundai are co-developing a fresh dedicated EV architecture for an upcoming pair of entry-level electric cars.

Expected to arrive as the Hyundai IONIQ 1 and Kia EV1, the new EVs will compete with other entry-level electric cars like the Renault Twingo, which starts at about €20,000.

It has been revealed that lee remarked the EV1’s price will be highly competitive not just with other entry-level EVs, but also with small gas-powered cars, with prices expected to start in the €20,000 to €22,000 range, or about $22,000 to $24,000. And that’s without government incentives.

The EV2 starts at just €26,600 ($29,500) in Germany and other European markets as Kia’s current entry-level EV, so the price range would make sense.

While it will be Kia’s cheapest EV, Lee promised it would not cut corners in quality, design, or features.

As its first SDV, the EV1 will feature Kia and Hyundai Motor’s latest-generation tech and software. Kia mentioned the electric SDV will offer Level 2+ autonomous driving on highways. In 2029, Kia intends to expand to Level 2++, enabling it to operate in cities.

The fresh EV will also use Hyundai’s SDV architecture (CODA), the Pleos Connect infotainment system, and Gleo AI, an in-vehicle Agenic AI.

What will the EV1 look like? According to Auto Express, the entry-level EV will look a bit sportier and less boxy than the EV2 SUV. It could draw inspiration from the Vision Meta Turismo concept.

Industry observers note that it also apparently won’t be based on the Picanto, Kia’s smallest gas-powered car. The Kia EV1 is expected to bring a unique style to the family.

Sources indicate that this is good to see and makes sense, especially in Europe. I don't think Kia can go wrong making vehicles at so many different price points. It allows them to reach different segments and almost literally have something for almost everyone.

While all of Kia’s current EVs feature its ccNC infotainment system with dual 12.3″ instrument display and infotainment screens, plus a 5″ climate control panel, the EV1 could bring a simpler setup.

Like its other electric models, the EV1 is expected to receive the GT treatment. However, as an entry-level model, it may not use a dual-motor all-wheel-drive setup like the others.

In a recent development, will Kia bring the EV1 to the US? Don’t get your hopes up. Kia has previously remarked the B-segment hatchback is designed for Europe. It could even be built alongside the EV2 at Kia’s plant in Slovakia.

The good news? The EV3, Kia’s compact electric SUV, is now on sale in the US, starting at just $29,890.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “Naming right whales is a fun and creative activity for our research community, but it also allows an opportunity to connect with the whales on an individual level,” Amy Warren, an aquarium scientific program officer and name project coordinator, said in Anderson Cabot Center’s announcement.
  • The 2026 inductees also include Grand Slam (Catalog #3991) and Slide (Catalog #4991).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Less than 400 adult North Atlantic right whales (Eubalaena glacialis) still exist in the wild, making them one of the world’s most critically endangered species. Of those, 20 have officially received spiffy new names from conservationists at the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center for Ocean Life. The researchers curate the annual North Atlantic Right Whale Catalog, and attach personable monikers to a select few baleen cetaceans in order to more easily monitor them. This year, it’s time to wave hello to Dodo, Volcano, and Dolly.

“Naming right whales is a fun and creative activity for our research community, but it also allows an opportunity to connect with the whales on an individual level,” Amy Warren, an aquarium scientific program officer and name project coordinator, said in Anderson Cabot Center’s announcement. “It can be hard to relate to Catalog #5299, but a whale named Nibbles is bound to be memorable.”.

The 2026 inductees also include Grand Slam (Catalog #3991) and Slide (Catalog #4991). The sister whales have a mother named Fenway (Catalog #2791), who was also named in honor of the Boston Red Sox. Grand Slam earned her newly introduced name thanks to her three patches of raised tissue known as callosities that resemble the bases on a baseball field. Meanwhile, Slide received their name due to the curved scar on her back that recalls someone sliding through home plate. Other right whale names this year include Goose, Donegal, and even Gonzo for the beloved Muppet.

“Although the names are intended to help researchers at sea, they also give the general public a better understanding of the individual whales,” added Caroline Mowdy, a spokesperson for Whale and Dolphin Conservation (WDC).

Industry observers note that collaborators at the WDC also created some lighthearted, yearbook-esque biographies for each whale. For example, Dolly (Catalog #4191), whose callosity looks strikingly similar to the late, great country singer’s larger-than-life hair, apparently loves the song, “Jolene.” Then again, who doesn’t?

“We see these whales and their families grow each year,” stated Mowdy. “Knowing them makes the tragedies even more tragic, but it also makes our determination to protect them even stronger.”.

Recent findings suggest that on Monday, the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium announced that there are roughly 382 North Atlantic right whales, representing a 1.8 percent drop in population size from the 2024 estimate. Their primary threats remain getting tangled in fishing line and vessel strikes.

However, even amid their struggles, the 2025–2026 right whale calving season saw the most calves born since 2009. A total of 24 calves were born, including a surprising late addition that was spotted in Canada in September.

#121282. What Children Really Notice About Honesty
