Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What a Missed Deadline Taught Me About Switching Off

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I missed a deadline last week.
  • The main problem was I simply ran out of time to write the piece.
  • The other problem and consequence was that I carried a chunk of guilt into the break.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I missed a deadline last week. The piece you’re reading was supposed to be filed before I headed out on a long weekend to Italy for my wife’s birthday.

The main problem was I simply ran out of time to write the piece. An urgent stakeholder ask out of the blue, a couple of unanticipated work fire drills, and a long-standing evening social commitment earlier in the week made for a perfect storm, and something had to give.

The other problem and consequence was that I carried a chunk of guilt into the break.

It caught up with me at 6 am on the first morning, when I found myself drafting this column in my head. I should have been dozing peacefully. I continued to ruminate on my lengthy to-do list at work deep into day one as we headed from Venice into the Dolomites. My body was in Italy, but my brain was clearly still at my desk.

Switching off, particularly from work, is hard for most of us, and especially in an age of ubiquitous screens and wall-to-wall information competing for our attention. For me, that always-on reality plays a major role in the difficulties I have disconnecting from the daily grind.

I’m fortunate to love my job, and if I’m candid, I probably take a little too much of my identity from it. I hold on tight, and the phone in my pocket is an ever-present enabler.

A meme that has stuck with me over the years goes something along the lines of being an adult is staring at medium screens all day only to come home and stare at a little screen while a massive screen is on in the background. The irony is not lost on me that I came across this rather withering take on modern life while scrolling on mentioned little screen.

Regardless of the role the screen plays, psychologists who study employee well-being describe what I was missing for the early part of the weekend as “psychological detachment.” A state where you are genuinely able to not think about work while away from it. The science suggests it’s an important thing to work on.

A 2025 meta-analysis of 32 studies found that vacationing has a strong effect on well-being, and that the effect lasts longer than earlier research suggested. A second, smaller analysis of eight studies points to detaching from work, along with physical activity, as among the most helpful things to do while you’re off. In another study that tracked teachers during a two-week break, exhaustion, anxiety, and low mood all declined, while those who kept ruminating about work recovered less.

Whatever the science claims, I know that for me the act of stepping away from work and being disciplined about not checking back in while I’m away is critical for my mental health and for staving off burnout. Getting out in nature and hiking or cycling or swimming keeps me present. It resets and recharges my batteries, and it tops up my creativity in a way that I find benefits what I am then able to bring back to the office.

Recent findings suggest that sure enough, as we drove deeper into the mountains on a crisp, blue-sky day, I could feel the golden autumnal hues and majestic rock formations drawing me in, closer to an elemental feeling of calm and happiness. That sense of equilibrium stayed with me all weekend, and while I’d be lying if I said my mind didn’t occasionally drift to my desk, it was fleeting, with the knowledge that all the things would be waiting for me when I got back. Just like this piece was.

With Thanksgiving on the horizon, and the holidays coming thick and fast thereafter, I’ll leave you with this bit of hard-earned advice: if your job is deeply entwined with your life and part of who you are, as mine is, time away can sometimes feel like a small act of disloyalty. It isn’t. In fact, it’s probably the most crucial thing you can do to remain faithful to your work ethic, and to yourself.

According to recent reports, and if you’ll be working over the holidays, or you’re not working right now, or you don’t have the benefit of someone on hand to carry some of the load for you (shout out to all the Grannies out there), or your vacation looks very different from mine, that’s all okay. Find the pockets where and when you can: an evening, a walk, an hour in front of a screen, or better yet a book, and let work wait. Above all else, be kind to yourself. That’s how you really give yourself a break.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

According to recent reports, as described in the article “In Fighting for Every Black Child, Did I Betray My Own?,” teenager Najya Hannah-Jones confronted her mother, the prominent journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones, about the choice to send her to public school in a system that, for many, provides substandard education. It was refreshing to read of Najya fighting to get a better education, a striking contrast with the popular but often inaccurate stereotype of lazy teens aiming to learn as little as possible. More importantly, kudos to Nikole Hannah-Jones for candidly admitting in her article that teachers lied to her about what they were teaching and, worse, tried to deceive both mother and daughter about what had actually been learned.

Every parent has a duty to nurture their children, but all parents also must consider their values when choosing schools for their children, so it is heartbreaking to realize that Ms. Hannah-Jones could have chosen a far better public school in New York for her daughter that would have met the core values listed in her article. Public school? Check. Racially diverse or perhaps even predominately Black student body? Check. Most importantly, a track record of meeting educational standards and being honest with parents regarding what their child is learning and how they are performing? Check and check.

Recent findings suggest that the truth is that Nikole Hannah-Jones could have enrolled her daughter in a local public school where the majority of students are Black and other nonwhite families and has long offered much better odds for positive educational outcomes. There has long been such an option available to parents that is too often ignored: Newly introduced York City charter schools.

In a recent development, in the book Charter Schools and Their Enemies, Thomas Sowell painstakingly and convincingly demonstrates that public charter schools in New York City consistently outperform neighborhood schools. Based on Ms. Hannah-Jones essay, one could argue that is not an especially high bar, but the data in the book show academic superiority relative to even the higher-quality schools in New York City, New York State, and nationwide. It is noteworthy that Sowell meticulously controls for the usual “straw men” used to assault charter schools. Indeed, some of the charter schools were not only in the same neighborhoods, but in the same building as the comparison schools in his study.

In a recent development, it is an ongoing tragedy that Ms. Hannah-Jones and others in the Black community are not demanding an expansion of public charter school options for their children. After all, and perhaps this is why they are under assault, public charter schools provide prima facia evidence that Latest York can, in fact, deliver a high-quality public education, but chooses not to do so. One hopes that other families like the Hannah-Joneses will enroll their children in public charter schools and demand that New York City be more honest what is being taught and what their children have learned.

The national discussion Ms. Hannah-Jones has sparked has been overwhelmingly focused on schools with majority Black student enrollment, but the debate should not be narrowly circumscribed. The truth is that every teen enrolled in failing schools across the U.S. should be asking their parents the same question Najya Hannah-Jones asked her mother: Why are you sending me to a school you already know is delivering a substandard education?

Stripped to essentials, Ms. Hannah-Jones faced the same choice most families do when deciding whether to enroll their children in public schools, regardless of race: If I send my child to the local school as a kindergartner, what is the probability that my child will emerge from 8th grade with the basic reading and math skills needed to succeed in high school and beyond? It turns out that there are ample data to help parents answer this question.

The National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) provides annual statistics on U.S. education outcomes. Nationally, only 26% of 8th-graders are proficient or above in math, according to its 2022 Nation's Report Card; only about one in four children are entering high school with grade-level proficiency in math. Reading outcomes are only slightly better, with 28% of 8th-graders being rated as proficient. Candidly, this is a national disgrace that poses an excruciating dilemma for parents and students.

It has been revealed that A usual response to this data is to argue that public schools are underfunded. Newly introduced York spends an average of more than $30,000 per student. Overall, the U.S. consistently spends more per pupil than nearly every other country in the world, including many that deliver better outcomes while paying less than half of what the U.S spends. More money is not translating to better outcomes. Does anyone believe that even doubling expenditures or even tripling them would appreciably improve outcomes at the school Najya Hannah-Jones attended, or any other failing school? After all, real spending, even adjusted for inflation, has more than doubled in the past 25 years and outcomes are actually a bit worse nationwide over the same period.

If it is not simply spending more money, what should parents do? The best answer: Do your homework. There are often options. Many states have adopted public options, including public charter schools, public magnet schools, and other similar approaches.

Several of my own children attended a public school implementing a Montessori teaching approach and two of my granddaughters are currently enrolled in a similar public school in Nashville. I was (and am) very pleased with what they were taught, how they were taught, and what they learned. Another daughter attended an academic magnet public high school that consistently outperforms even the most expensive private schools, even though, in general, Nashville public schools often have relatively poor outcomes for most students. The evidence is overwhelming that public school systems know how to deliver a high-quality education. Why are they choosing not to? Najya Hannah-Jones is absolutely right to demand answers and all teens—and their parents—should be asking the same questions.

Sowell, T. (2020). Charter schools and their enemies. Basic Books.
